newsitem.title: USA: U.S. and Europe strike barter deal on space station.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and Europe strike barter deal on space station.

text.p: Europe will build two docking modules for the planned international space station in exchange for a free ride for a European laboratory on the space shuttle, NASA said on Monday.
Under the barter deal, the Columbus laboratory, Europe's main contribution to the $60 billion space station, will be launched on the U.S. shuttle in late 2002 or early 2003.

In return the European Space Agency will provide two modules called nodes needed to link the station's laboratory and habitation modules. The first, scheduled for launch in mid-2000, will replace a U.S.-built component that suffered structural problems.

Europe had been considering launching the laboratory on the troubled Ariane 5 rocket but the costs and risks involved appeared prohibitive. ESA officials said construction of the nodes is to be delegated to the Italian Space Agency, which had complained it was not receiving enough contracts in return for its financial contribution to the 14-member space agency.
"With this solution, everyone gains", Jorg Feustel-Buechl, ESA's director of manned spaceflight and microgravity, said in a statement.
As part of the deal, ESA will also provide freezers for the station's U.S. habitation and laboratory modules and a variety of other laboratory equipment.

The space station project brings together space programmes of the United States, Russia, Japan, Europe and Canada to construct the orbiting outpost, which will weigh close to a million pounds (455,000 kg) and stretch longer than a football field.
Construction of the station was supposed to get under way in November but Russian financial difficulties were likely to force a delay of at least six months.
